step: 6.8 phase 4: HTTP/1.1 and h2c transport comparison with equal initial stock
method: Two sequential owned disposable kind labs from the same commit and images. Values = kind-values.yaml + orderProducer.configuration.SHARDSHOP_PRODUCER_ORDER_RATE "0"; lab B adds httpBalancer.workloadProtocol H2C. The retained lab was stopped during both labs.

host.note: Heavy host paging in every phase of both labs (full-phase swap traffic 3.5-11.8 GB in lab A, 2.7-8.9 GB in lab B); paging is diagnostic only, as in the 2026-10-28 runs.

failedAttemptLabB: First lab B up.sh stopped in the build: OrderHttp2Test.requiresADeclaredLengthForHttp2Bodies read the body on the test thread after the response future completed, and Vert.x dropped the data (empty body). A 300 ms pause reproduced it every time. Both HTTP/2 tests now read the body in the response callback; the lab was destroyed and lab B ran again (b2) with the same images.
outcome: Not qualified for either transport under this host paging. In lab B, one low 30-second read window failed the 750/s and 1,000/s targets, and 10 writes/s missed 95% delivery. h2c above 1,000 reads/s is not measured. Superseded by phase 4d (repeatAfterDockerRestart), which repeated both labs with low host paging.
limitations: Host swap traffic of 3.5-11.8 GB (lab A) and 2.7-8.9 GB (lab B) per phase; write latencies are not comparable with the 2026-10-28 operating points. Corrected 2026-10-30: the first record measured only to the lexically last sample (sample-90 of 0-150), thus it gave lower values.
Lab B stopped the write sequence after 10/s (delivery 94.6%), thus 20/s and 30/s have no h2c result.

Phase 4b profile (retained lab, 2026-10-30): at 1,000 reads/s the HttpCore I/O thread used 8.1% of one core, the reader delivered 987.0/s, and no reader thread was RUNNABLE in three dumps. Thus the lab B failures came from one low window per target, not from a steady client limit; their cause is not known.
One run per transport; no repeat.
Phase 4c (diagnostic): on the retained H2C lab the read search passed 4,000/s (3,936-3,942/s per window); 8,000/s and 6,000/s failed with the reader at up to 14 of 16 streams.

retainedLabH2cReadSearch.kind: diagnostic, not a qualified comparison (retained lab, different data and host paging)

repeatAfterDockerRestart.method: The user quit other applications and approved a Docker Desktop restart. The retained lab was stopped (down.sh), Docker Desktop was restarted before each lab (docker desktop restart), then lab.sh ran lab A2 (HTTP_1_1) and lab B3 (H2C) with the unchanged phase 4 values, collectors and image digests.
repeatAfterDockerRestart.outcome: Both transports met the write criteria at 10, 20 and 30 orders/s (HTTP_1_1 p95 25.6-29.3 ms, H2C p95 31.3-32.8 ms). Highest passing read target: HTTP_1_1 8,000/s (7,843.9/s), H2C 6,000/s (5,868.6/s); H2C at 8,000/s delivered 7,589.7/s with two of three windows below 7,600/s.
findings: The phase 4 read failures of lab B (750 and 1,000/s) did not repeat with low host paging; they probably came from paging.

At 8,000 reads/s the H2C reader leased 13-16 of its 16 streams, the HTTP_1_1 reader 6-8 of its 16 connections: each h2c read holds its lease approximately twice as long (extra Envoy hop), thus the reader pool size limits h2c reads.
One Envoy pod carried the reads (max 568 millicores of a 2-core limit, 22 MiB); the other pod max 59 millicores.
Reader retried transport errors before the read search: 128 in lab B3, 6 in lab A2; no error in any selected window.
limitations: Write paging 0.4-1.0 GB per phase in lab A2, above the 256 MiB diagnostic reference; read paging up to 0.25 GB except 2.8 GB at 10,000/s.

h2cSaturationSearch.method: User decision after phase 4d: one disposable H2C lab with the lab B3 values plus productReader.configuration SHARDSHOP_READER_WORKERS "32" and SHARDSHOP_READER_CONNECTIONS "32" (the reader RUNBOOK raises both for saturation tests). The rendered application release differs from lab B3 only in these two variables. down.sh, then docker desktop restart before the lab; unchanged lab.sh, collectors, images and initial stock.
h2cSaturationSearch.outcome: With 32 workers and streams, H2C passed reads up to 8,000/s (7,678.5/s), as HTTP_1_1 with 16 in lab A2 (7,843.9/s). Both failed 9,000/s at nearly the same rate (H2C 8,469.3/s, HTTP_1_1 8,455.9/s); at 10,000/s H2C delivered 9,232.1/s and HTTP_1_1 8,759.6/s. Writes passed at 10, 20 and 30/s (p95 33.4, 53.0, 52.0 ms).
findings: The reader pool of 16 was the h2c read limit in lab B3; with 32 the pool held at most 28 leases.
Near 9,000/s all reader workers were busy at times in both labs (16 of 16 for HTTP_1_1, 32 of 32 for H2C), and the kind nodes used 6.2-7.7 of 12 CPUs; the limit at 9,000/s is not identified.
H2C read p95 at 8,000/s was 5 ms (2 ms with HTTP_1_1); write p95 was higher than in lab B3 at 20 and 30/s, but below 100 ms.
One Envoy pod carried the reads: max 584 millicores of 2 cores and 35.9 MiB; the other pod max 8 millicores.
The reader retried 192 transport errors during up.sh, before the measurement (128 in lab B3, 6 in lab A2); the cause is not examined.
limitations: Only H2C with 32; HTTP_1_1 with 32 is not measured.
